name: Thule people
info: The Thule, or proto-Inuit, were Arctic whale hunters who arose in coastal Alaska by 1000 CE and spread east across northern Canada to Greenland by the 13th century, becoming the ancestors of all Inuit and Yupik peoples.

facts.homeland: Coastal Alaska and the Bering Strait, then the Canadian Arctic (Baffin Island, Hudson Bay, Foxe Basin, the Mackenzie Delta) and Greenland; named after Thule (Pituffik) in north-west Greenland, where Comer’s Midden was dug.
facts.period: Forerunners: Old Bering Sea c. 200 BCE–500 CE, Punuk and Birnirk c. 800–1400 CE; eastward spread from c. 1000 CE; Classic Thule 1100–1400 CE; Post-Classic 1400–1600 CE, when local Inuit groups emerged.
facts.known: bowhead whaling from skin boats; dog sleds, kayaks and umiaks; semi-subterranean houses framed with whale bone; polished-slate tools and the ulu knife; meteoric and Norse iron; the eastward migration that replaced the Dorset culture
facts.sources: Excavated houses, middens and tools (the Fifth Thule Expedition of 1921–1924 and later digs); Norse sources, which call Arctic peoples Skrælingjar; genetic studies of Thule burials (2014) and of Arctic ancestry (2019).

t: The Thule were the direct ancestors of the Inuit and Yupik, who developed in coastal Alaska by 1000 CE and in a few centuries spread across the Canadian Arctic to Greenland.
Bowhead whales were at the heart of Classic Thule life, hunted by cooperating boat crews under a captain, the umialik, and used for food, fuel, house frames and tools.
Dog sleds, kayaks and large skin boats let the Thule range far and trade widely, and they displaced the earlier Dorset people across the eastern Arctic.
dyk: Long before European contact the Thule worked iron, some of it from meteorites such as the Cape York meteorite in Greenland and some traded from the Norse.
ev: The Old Bering Sea stage, an early phase of the Thule Tradition, begins around the Bering Strait
The Punuk and Birnirk stages develop on the Bering Strait islands and the coasts of northern and western Alaska
Thule culture has developed in coastal Alaska, and Thule groups begin moving east across the Canadian Arctic
The Norse reach the shores of Canada, and contact with the Thule follows
Thule populations have largely replaced the Dorset people of northern Canada and Greenland
Colder climate ends whaling from boats in the High Arctic, which the Thule abandon; local Inuit groups emerge
Therkel Mathiassen of the Fifth Thule Expedition excavates sites and maps out the Thule culture

sections.origins:
The Thule, also called the proto-Inuit, were the forerunners of all modern Inuit and Yupik peoples. Their name is an archaeologists’ label taken from Thule, now Pituffik, in north-west Greenland, where their remains were first found at Comer’s Midden. The culture was mapped out by the archaeologist and cartographer Therkel Mathiassen, who took part in the Fifth Thule Expedition led by Knud Rasmussen in 1921–1924. He excavated sites on Baffin Island and around north-western Hudson Bay and argued, correctly, that they were the remains of a whaling culture that had begun in Alaska and moved into Arctic Canada about a thousand years earlier.

Archaeologists trace a longer Thule Tradition around the Bering Strait from about 200 BCE to 1600 CE, in stages often called “Neo-Eskimo” to set them apart from the earlier Norton tradition. The Old Bering Sea stage, first described by Diamond Jenness from decorated ivory harpoon heads found on the St. Lawrence and Diomede Islands, ran from about 200 BCE to 500 CE; how it relates to the Okvik style is still debated. The Punuk stage, defined by Henry Collins in 1928 from a deep midden on the Punuk Islands, and the Birnirk stage of coastal northern and western Alaska followed from about 800 CE.

Digs on St. Lawrence Island showed an unbroken sequence from Old Bering Sea through Punuk to later Inuit culture. Genetic studies add to the picture. A 2019 analysis concluded that the ancestors of the Thule emerged in Alaska between 2,700 and 4,900 years ago from a mixing of Paleo-Eskimo and Ocean Bay Tradition peoples, moved back to Siberia and later returned. A 2014 study of Thule burials found that they descended from Birnirk populations of north-western Alaska, whose roots lay in north-eastern Siberia.
sections.society:
Thule life differed sharply from that of the earlier Dorset people of the eastern Arctic. Access to bowhead whales let some Thule communities grow into the largest settlements of the prehistoric Arctic: in the best whaling areas a village usually held fifteen to twenty houses, and at least one known site had sixty. Houses often stood in clusters that may have sheltered extended families, and archaeologists have identified communal buildings that seem to have been used for ceremonies.

Not every household had the same standing. Differences in the size, form and contents of houses, including whaling gear and goods from far away, may reflect differences of wealth or rank between families, and some researchers see in them signs of hierarchy within certain communities. Open-sea whaling needed the coordinated work of several crews and skilled leadership; in some communities the hunt was directed by a captain, the umialik, a position still prominent in Alaskan Arctic communities today. One hunter struck the whale while others attached floats to slow and hold it, and once ashore its meat, blubber and bone were shared out through the community.

In winter the Thule lived in semi-subterranean houses, often framed with whale jawbones and covered with skins, sod and snow; in summer they moved into skin tents whose edges were held down by circles of stones. Eastern houses were rounder and more above ground, with stone sleeping platforms. A single whale gave meat for food, blubber for light and cooking, and bone for houses and tools. Away from the great whaling places, people relied heavily on fish, large marine mammals and caribou, and they tried to use as much of every animal as they could.
sections.beliefs:
The archaeological record gives only a few clues to what the Thule believed, and any picture of their religion rests on inference. The communal structures found among clusters of houses appear to have been used for ceremonial activities. Whaling, too, depended on cooperation, and a whale’s meat, blubber and bone were distributed through the community once it was ashore.

Thule art offers further hints. The Old Bering Sea stage decorated its tools with flowing curvilinear designs of dots, circles and short lines, which make its objects easy to recognise; Punuk art became simpler and more standardised, and the Birnirk people decorated almost nothing beyond spiral and concentric patterns on clay pots. Classic Thule artists put simple linear designs on household objects such as combs, showing people without arms or legs, animals and other figures. Archaeologists note that the Classic Thule placed much emphasis on the practical use of art; what these images meant to their makers is not known.
sections.arts:
Thule technology was built for a life at sea and on the ice. Kayaks and umiaks, large boats of skin on a frame, first appear in the archaeological record in the Old Bering Sea stage, and the umiak became central to bowhead whaling. Tool kits were dominated by polished slate rather than flaked stone: lance-shaped knives, projectile heads and the ulu, a knife with a blade set across the handle. The people of the Bering Strait also made a simple pottery and used bone and antler for harpoon heads, darts, spears, snow goggles, blubber scrapers, needles, awls and mattocks, and walrus shoulder blades for snow shovels.

Hunting tools grew more effective over time. Harpoons carried ice picks for seal hunting, and ivory plugs and mouthpieces were used to inflate floats on the harpoon line, so that large sea mammals could be held and recovered. The Punuk stage added armour made of bone, the bow and arrow, bone wrist guards, reinforced bows, bird bolas, heavy ivory net sinkers and blunt bird arrows, and engraved its tools with iron-tipped points. Birnirk people used sledges of the same basic design as the later dog sleds, and their harpoon heads, more often of antler than ivory, changed in shape from phase to phase.

Dog sleds, kayaks and umiaks let Thule hunters follow migrating game and sea mammals over great distances and carry heavy loads. The Thule worked iron long before European contact, carving and engraving with it: some came from meteorites, such as the Cape York meteorite in Greenland, and some through trade from the Norse, and they hammered the raw iron into tools themselves, though supply was never steady. In the east, people preferred soapstone household vessels to pottery.
sections.exchange:
Around the beginning of the second millennium CE, Thule people began moving east. While western groups settled the northern and western coasts of Alaska, others crossed the Canadian Arctic as far as Greenland, which they reached by the 13th century. The distribution of early Alaskan-style harpoon heads shows two routes: one along the Beaufort Sea coast and Amundsen Gulf into the High Arctic through Parry Channel and Smith Sound, the other south along the western coast of Hudson Bay. In the same period the use of polished slate and Thule methods of making pottery spread west to the Aleutian Islands and southern Alaska.

Why they moved is debated. R. McGhee’s cultural-ecological model holds that the first families followed bowhead whales, whose summer range spread east during a warm period between 900 and 1200 that reduced the pack ice. Other explanations point to warfare in Alaska or the search for new sources of iron. Wherever they went, the Thule displaced the Dorset people who had occupied the central and eastern Canadian Arctic: by about 1300 CE they had largely replaced them, and by the 15th century entirely. Evidence of contact between the two is scarce, the 2014 genetic study found the Thule genetically distinct from the Dorset, and how the succession happened remains poorly understood.

The Thule, and to a lesser degree the Dorset, were also in contact with the Norse, who reached the shores of Canada in the 11th century; Norse sources call these peoples the Skrælingjar. Iron reached the Thule through Norse trade, yet the 2014 study found no sign of mixing between the Thule and the Greenlandic Norse, though both lived on the island for several centuries. Among the Thule themselves, native copper from the western Arctic and meteoric iron from north-western Greenland passed from community to community.
sections.legacy:
Classic Thule culture, between 1100 and 1400 CE, spread across the High Arctic and south to the coasts of Hudson Strait, Hudson Bay, Foxe Basin and the mainland from the Mackenzie Delta to the Melville Peninsula. Then the climate turned. A colder period between 1400 and 1600 limited the use of boats, reduced the number of whales and shortened the open-water hunting season. By the 16th century whaling from umiaks and kayaks had ended in the High Arctic, and by 1600 people had left the High Arctic altogether. Where whales were scarce, Post-Classic communities lived more on caribou, seal and fish; those near open water suffered less from the cold.

Out of these changes came the local groups known from later history, among them the Copper Inuit, the Netsilik and the Inuit of the Igloolik area. Contact with Europeans grew in the 18th century, and together with the disruption already caused by the cold of the Little Ice Age it broke the Thule communities apart. Their descendants became known to outsiders as Eskimo, a term now considered offensive, and later by their own names, Inuit and Yupik.

The Thule are thus not a vanished people but the ancestors of the Inuit and Yupik of today. Most of the Thule individuals sampled by geneticists belonged to the maternal lineage A2a, and the umialik, the whaling captain of Thule times, is still a prominent figure in Alaskan Arctic communities. The Thule migration, which carried one way of life from Alaska to Greenland in a few centuries, was the subject of the Canadian documentary Inuit Odyssey, first broadcast in 2009.

summary: The Thule were the proto-Inuit, Arctic hunters who developed in coastal Alaska by 1000 CE and within a few centuries spread across northern Canada to Greenland, replacing the Dorset culture. Their life centred on bowhead whaling from skin boats, dog sleds and houses framed with whale bone. A colder climate after 1400 broke up the old whaling life, and their descendants are the Inuit and Yupik of today.

notes: The saved article’s References and Sources sections are empty; the four references are its Further reading list, not footnoted citations.

Dates kept: start 1000 (the article: “developed in coastal Alaska by 1000 CE”), end 1600 (end of the Post-Classic stage and of the Thule Tradition’s span). The article also gives the Thule Tradition as c. 200 BCE–1600 CE; the earlier stages are treated as forerunners.

Conflict inside the article: the lede dates the Little Ice Age to 1650–1850, the Post-Classic section to 1400–1600. I wrote “a colder period between 1400 and 1600” for the Thule decline and “the Little Ice Age” without dates for the 18th-century break-up.

The article says the Thule Tradition “spread westward” between 900 and 1100 CE (to the Aleutians and southern Alaska) in a section headed western and eastern Arctic; I kept that westward spread of slate and pottery separate from the eastward migration.

The article’s sentence on the name is garbled (“Thule, now known as Pituffik (a settlement relocated and renamed Qaanaaq in 1953)”); I wrote only “Thule, now Pituffik, in north-west Greenland” and left out Qaanaaq.

Beliefs: the article says almost nothing about Thule religion. The section rests on what it does say (ceremonial communal structures, art styles, cooperative whaling and sharing, burials in the 2014 study) and states plainly that it is inference; it is the shortest section and the editor may want to trim it further rather than pad it.
The DNA study is dated August 2014 in Science; I did not name its authors (the article does not).
No museum or UNESCO listing is named in the article. Inuit Odyssey (CBC, 29 June 2009) comes from the article’s external links.
